title: Why Do We Dream?
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: For most of history, dreams were thought to carry messages from gods, spirits or the dead. The ancient Egyptians recorded dreams on papyrus, and the Greeks built temples where the sick slept in the hope of receiving a cure from a dream. It was only in the twentieth century that dreaming became a subject of laboratory research, after scientists discovered a stage of sleep in which the eyes move rapidly beneath the lids and the brain is almost as active as when awake.

This stage, known as REM sleep, was identified in 1953 at the University of Chicago. Subjects woken during REM sleep reported vivid dreams about four times out of five, while those woken at other times rarely did. We now know that the typical adult has four or five REM periods each night, and that the longest, towards morning, can last nearly an hour. During REM the body is almost paralysed, which prevents us from acting out our dreams, although in some people this mechanism fails.

Why we dream remains unknown, and several theories compete. Freud argued that dreams express hidden wishes that the mind has pushed out of everyday thought, but his ideas have little support from modern experiments. A second theory, known as activation-synthesis, proposes that dreams are the brain's attempt to make sense of random electrical signals produced during sleep. Critics point out that dreams are often far more organised and emotional than random signals would produce, and that the theory does not explain why the same themes recur.

A third theory, which has attracted much attention, says that dreaming helps memory. During sleep, the brain replays the events of the day and decides which to keep, and dreams may be the conscious side of that process. In one experiment, volunteers who dreamed about a maze they had been learning performed much better when tested later than those who did not. Not everyone accepts the explanation, and some researchers argue that dreams are a by-product, like the noise of a machine, with no function of their own.

A fourth theory suggests that dreams are a kind of rehearsal for threats. The Finnish researcher Antti Revonsuo has proposed that our ancestors who dreamed about danger became better at facing it, and that natural selection therefore favoured dreaming. The theory fits the fact that dreams so often contain fear, chase and failure, even in the lives of people who are safe and comfortable. On the other hand, many dreams are quite ordinary, and some contain pleasant or silly events that have no obvious survival value.

Some people can control their dreams. In a lucid dream, the sleeper knows that he or she is dreaming and may be able to change what happens. Researchers have shown that lucid dreamers can send signals to the laboratory by moving their eyes in a pre-arranged pattern, which proves that they are aware during the dream. Some athletes and musicians practise their skills in lucid dreams, and early results suggest that this may help real performance, although the research is limited and the numbers of people tested are small.

Whatever their purpose, dreams remain a source of fascination. Writers, scientists and artists have credited dreams with ideas: the chemist Kekulé said that the shape of the benzene ring came to him in a dream, and Mary Shelley said that the idea for Frankenstein came to her in one. Most researchers today are cautious about claims that a particular dream has a fixed meaning. As Professor Hannah Lindqvist puts it, 'a dream is not a message to be decoded but an experience to be understood.'
